fields.meta_title: Testimonial Form Builder With Questions to Ask | Emergent
fields.meta_description: What a testimonial form asks, the questions that produce a quote worth publishing, and a free builder that records permission with every answer.
fields.h1: Build a Testimonial Form That Gets Quotes You Can Publish
fields.hero_description: A testimonial form asks a happy customer what changed and whether you may quote it. Describe yours, and Emergent builds it with a permission step and a database you own.
fields.features_heading: What a Testimonial Form Should Do
fields.features_subheading: Templates collect the words. Emergent's version also keeps the permission and the edits behind every quote.
fields.feature_1:
Questions in story order

Asks what the problem was before, then what changed and what result followed. Answers given in that order read as a story, and the result line is often the one you quote.
fields.feature_2:
A permission choice on every answer

Lets the customer pick how their name appears and whether a photo may run beside the quote. Both choices, with the date they were made, sit on the same row as the testimonial.
fields.feature_3:
Client approval of the edited quote

Emails the trimmed quote back to the customer with Approve and Suggest a change buttons. A quote is never marked ready to publish until the customer who wrote it says yes.
fields.feature_4:
Photo and video uploads

Accepts a headshot or a short video clip in the same form, from any phone. Files are stored next to the written answer in storage you own, named with the customer and the date.
fields.feature_5:
A searchable library of quotes

Saves each testimonial with tags for the product and the industry. Sales can filter by any tag and copy an approved quote into a proposal without waiting on the marketing team.
fields.feature_6:
Your code, in your repo

Exports the full app to your GitHub on paid plans. A developer can feed approved quotes to your website through the API, or you can describe the change and let Emergent write it.

fields.usecase_heading: Testimonial Forms by Who Gives the Quote
fields.tab_content_1:
The client signs off on every edited quote

Clients answer in paragraphs, and a homepage has room for two sentences. When Fernhill Studio closes a website project, the client answers 3 questions about the old site and the results. Marketing trims them into a two-sentence quote and emails it back. It is ready to publish only after the client clicks Approve.
fields.tab_content_2:
Coaching clients pick which name runs beside a quote

Some clients praise a coach in public, and some only in private. At the end of a 12-week program, the form asks how the client's name may appear, with a separate yes or no for a photo. Dev Malhotra chose first name and initial with no photo, and the site shows Dev M.
fields.tab_content_3:
Seller quotes filed by neighborhood for the next pitch

Sellers trust what their neighbors said about an agent. The form goes out the day each sale closes, and every quote is saved with its neighborhood and price band. Before a listing appointment in Cedar Park, the agent filters the library and gets 3 approved quotes from Cedar Park sellers.
fields.tab_content_4:
Every $15 credit is disclosed under its quote

A store credit changes what a reader needs to know about a quote. Juniper Skin gives each customer who submits a testimonial $15 in store credit, whatever the rating. The form records the credit on the testimonial's row, and the product page prints "Received $15 store credit" under that quote.

fields.howto_title: How to Create a Testimonial Form
fields.howto_description: Good testimonials come from a specific question, asked at the right moment, with permission on file. Seven steps, in the order you will need them.
fields.howto_step_1_title: 01 Decide where the quotes will run
fields.howto_step_4_title: 04 Ask for permission in plain words
fields.howto_step_1_des: Pick the first place testimonials will appear, such as the homepage or sales proposals. Placement sets the length you need and whether a photo matters. A homepage quote runs two sentences, while a proposal can carry a full paragraph with numbers.
fields.howto_step_2_des: Ask for a figure the customer can stand behind, such as hours saved each week or days cut from a deadline. A number in their own words outweighs any adjective. If they have none, ask what they would tell a colleague who is considering you.
fields.howto_step_3_des: Every question you add costs answers. Two or three open questions, one rating and a consent choice cover most needs. Put the optional photo or video upload after the written answers. A camera prompt halfway through stalls people before they finish.
fields.howto_step_4_des: Say where the quote may run and how the name will appear, then let the customer choose. Name the places, such as your website and paid ads, instead of any marketing purpose. A checkbox buried in small print leaves you no record that anyone read it.
fields.howto_step_5_title: 05 Send it the week the result shows
fields.howto_step_5_des: Time the request to the moment the customer feels the result, such as the week a site launches or the last session of a program. Ask months later and the answer comes back vaguer, if it comes back at all.
fields.howto_step_6_title: 06 Edit lightly and send it back
fields.howto_step_6_des: Trim for length and fix typos, but keep the customer's meaning. The FTC's guides allow rewording only when it does not distort the endorser's opinion. Send the edited version back for approval before it goes on your site.
fields.howto_step_7_des: A discount or free product given for a testimonial is a connection the FTC expects you to disclose next to the quote. Offer it for any honest answer. Its rule on reviews bars rewarding only the positive ones.
